```{r install-package, include = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
# Run once in the console if xaringan is not installed
install.packages("xaringan")
```

```{r load-packages, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(knitr)
library(xaringanthemer)
```

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.retina = 3, dpi = 300, fig.width = 6, fig.asp = 0.618,
  out.width = "80%", echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE
)
options(scipen = 999)
```

```{r load-data, include = FALSE}
rawdata <- read_csv("data/ames.csv")
```

```{r prep-data, include = FALSE}
# Same preparation as the investigation worksheet
data <- rawdata %>%
  select(price, area, Year.Built, Yr.Sold, Year.Remod.Add, Bedroom.AbvGr,
         Overall.Qual, Overall.Cond, Garage.Cars, Fireplaces, Kitchen.AbvGr,
         Full.Bath, Half.Bath) %>%
  rename(bedrooms = Bedroom.AbvGr, kitchens = Kitchen.AbvGr) %>%
  mutate(
    Remod.Year.Vs.Year.Sold  = Yr.Sold - Year.Remod.Add,
    Remod.Year.Vs.Year.Built = Year.Remod.Add - Year.Built,
    If.Remodelled = case_when(
      Remod.Year.Vs.Year.Built == 0 ~ "No",
      Remod.Year.Vs.Year.Built > 0  ~ "Yes"
    ),
    bathrooms = Full.Bath + 0.5 * Half.Bath
  ) %>%
  na.omit()

median_price <- median(data$price)
mean_price   <- mean(data$price)
sd_price     <- sd(data$price)
median_area  <- median(data$area)

cor_area  <- cor(data$price, data$area)
cor_built <- cor(data$price, data$Year.Built)
cor_remod <- cor(data$price, data$Year.Remod.Add)
cor_bed   <- cor(data$price, data$bedrooms)
cor_area_bed <- cor(data$area, data$bedrooms)

full_lm  <- lm(price ~ area + bedrooms + Overall.Qual + Overall.Cond + kitchens + bathrooms,
               data = data)
final_lm <- lm(price ~ area + bedrooms + Overall.Qual + kitchens, data = data)

final_coef <- tidy(final_lm)
final_fit  <- glance(final_lm)
coef_of <- function(term_name) final_coef$estimate[final_coef$term == term_name]

resid <- augment(final_lm, data = data)

dollar <- scales::dollar
```

class: center, middle

## How much do different features of a house affect its sale price in Ames, Iowa?

---

# Our question

.pull-left[
**Which characteristics of a house best explain its sale price?**

We looked at:

- **Size**: living area, bedrooms, bathrooms, kitchens
- **Age**: year built, year sold
- **Renovation**: whether and when the house was remodelled
- **Quality**: overall quality and condition ratings (1 to 10)
]

.pull-right[
Our approach:

1. Explore each variable against price
2. Fit a multiple linear regression
3. Keep only the significant predictors
4. Check the model with its residuals
]

---

# The data

- Ames Housing data: **`r format(nrow(data), big.mark = ",")` house sales** in Ames, Iowa (`r min(data$Yr.Sold)` to `r max(data$Yr.Sold)`), after removing rows with missing values

- **Response:** `price`, the sale price in US dollars

- **Variables we created:**
  - `bathrooms` = full baths + 0.5 × half baths (a half bath has a toilet and sink but no bath or shower)
  - `If.Remodelled`: "Yes" if the remodel year differs from the build year
  - Years between building and remodelling, and between remodelling and sale

---

# How are house prices distributed?

.pull-left[
```{r price-density, out.width = "100%", fig.width = 5}
ggplot(data, aes(x = price)) +
  geom_density(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = median_price, colour = "red",
             linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_price, colour = "orange",
             linewidth = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, max(data$price), by = 100000),
                     labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
  labs(title = "Density of house prices",
       subtitle = "Red = median, orange = mean",
       x = "House price ($)", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()
```
]

.pull-right[
- Median price: **`r dollar(median_price)`**
- Mean price: **`r dollar(round(mean_price))`**
- Standard deviation: `r dollar(round(sd_price))`

<br>

Prices are **right-skewed**: most houses sell for moderate prices, while a small number of very expensive houses pull the mean above the median.
]

---

# Reading the numbers: correlation (r)

.pull-left[
The **correlation coefficient r** measures how closely two variables follow a straight line.

- It runs from **-1 to +1**
- **+1**: perfect positive link (one goes up, the other goes up)
- **-1**: perfect negative link
- **0**: no straight-line link at all
- Rough guide: about 0.1 is weak, 0.3 moderate, 0.5 or more strong
]

.pull-right[
**r tells us about association, not cause.** A high r does not prove that one thing causes the other.

r only captures *straight-line* patterns, and outliers can push it up or down.

**R²** (used in our model) is closely linked: with one predictor, R² = r². It is the share of the variation in price that the model explains.
]

---

# Bigger houses sell for more

.pull-left[
```{r price-area, out.width = "100%", fig.width = 5}
ggplot(data, aes(x = area, y = price)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue", size = 1.5, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "red") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(title = "House price vs living area",
       x = "Above-ground living area (sq ft)", y = "House price") +
  theme_minimal()
```
]

.pull-right[
- Strongest single relationship we found: correlation **r = `r round(cor_area, 2)`**

- On its own, area explains about **`r round(100 * glance(lm(price ~ area, data = data))$r.squared)`%** of the variation in price

- Spread gets wider for larger houses (a "cone" shape), so big houses are harder to predict
]

---

# Newer and renovated houses sell for more

.pull-left[
```{r price-built, out.width = "100%", fig.width = 5}
ggplot(data, aes(x = Year.Built, y = price)) +
  geom_point(colour = "darkgreen", size = 1.5, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "red") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(title = "House price vs year built",
       x = "Year built", y = "House price") +
  theme_minimal()
```
- Year built: r = `r round(cor_built, 2)`
- Year of last remodel: r = `r round(cor_remod, 2)`
]

.pull-right[
```{r price-remodelled, out.width = "100%", fig.width = 5}
ggplot(data, aes(x = If.Remodelled, y = price)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "darkmagenta", alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(title = "Remodelled vs not remodelled",
       x = "Has the house been remodelled?", y = "House price") +
  theme_minimal()
```
- Both age variables have weaker links to price than area
]

---

# Do more bedrooms mean a higher price?

.pull-left[
```{r price-bedrooms, out.width = "100%", fig.width = 5}
ggplot(data, aes(x = factor(bedrooms), y = price)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "yellow", colour = "red", alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(title = "House price vs bedrooms",
       x = "Number of bedrooms", y = "House price") +
  theme_minimal()
```
]

.pull-right[
- Price barely rises with bedrooms: **r = `r round(cor_bed, 2)`**, a weak positive link

- But bedrooms and living area move together (r = `r round(cor_area_bed, 2)`): houses with more bedrooms tend to be bigger

- So some of the "bedroom effect" is really a size effect. This matters for the model later.
]

---

class: inverse, center, middle

# Putting it together: multiple regression

---

# Reading the numbers: p-values

.pull-left[
Each coefficient in a regression comes with a **p-value**.

- We start by assuming the variable has **no effect** on price once the others are accounted for (the *null hypothesis*)
- The p-value is the chance of seeing an effect at least as big as ours **if that assumption were true**
- **Small p-value** = our result would be very unlikely if there were no real effect
]

.pull-right[
We use a **5% significance level**:

- **p < 0.05**: evidence of a real relationship, so we keep the variable
- **p ≥ 0.05**: not enough evidence, so we drop it

For example, overall condition had **p = `r round(tidy(full_lm)$p.value[tidy(full_lm)$term == "Overall.Cond"], 3)`**, so there is no evidence it affects price once size and quality are known.

A p-value does **not** tell us how *big* or how *important* an effect is. That comes from the coefficient.
]

---

# Our final model

We started with area, bedrooms, overall quality, overall condition, kitchens and bathrooms. **Overall condition and bathrooms were not significant** at the 5% level, so we dropped them.

```{r final-model-table}
final_coef %>%
  mutate(
    term = recode(term,
      "(Intercept)" = "Intercept", "area" = "Area (per sq ft)",
      "bedrooms" = "Bedrooms", "Overall.Qual" = "Overall quality (per point)",
      "kitchens" = "Kitchens"),
    across(c(estimate, std.error), ~ round(.x, 1)),
    statistic = round(statistic, 2),
    p.value = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, "< 0.001", as.character(round(p.value, 3)))
  ) %>%
  kable(format = "html",
        col.names = c("Term", "Estimate ($)", "Std. error", "t", "p-value"))
```

<br>

**R² = `r round(final_fit$r.squared, 3)`**: the model explains about **`r round(100 * final_fit$r.squared)`%** of the variation in price (the full six-variable model gave `r round(summary(full_lm)$r.squared, 3)`, so the dropped variables added almost nothing).

---

# What the coefficients tell us

Holding the other variables constant:

- **Overall quality** is the strongest effect: each extra point adds about **`r dollar(round(coef_of("Overall.Qual")))`** (t ≈ `r round(final_coef$statistic[final_coef$term == "Overall.Qual"], 1)`)

- **Area**: each extra square foot adds about **`r dollar(round(coef_of("area"), 2))`**

- **Bedrooms**: each extra bedroom *lowers* the price by about **`r dollar(round(abs(coef_of("bedrooms"))))`**

- **Kitchens**: each extra kitchen *lowers* the price by about **`r dollar(round(abs(coef_of("kitchens"))))`**

--

**Why negative?** The model already controls for area. For two houses of the *same size*, more bedrooms means smaller rooms. A second kitchen often signals a house split into flats or an older conversion, which buyers may value less.

The intercept (`r dollar(round(coef_of("(Intercept)")))`) has no real meaning, since no house has zero area.

---

# Checking the model

.pull-left[
```{r resid-fitted, out.width = "100%", fig.width = 5}
ggplot(resid, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs fitted values",
       x = "Fitted price", y = "Residual") +
  theme_minimal()
```
]

.pull-right[
```{r resid-hist, out.width = "100%", fig.width = 5}
ggplot(resid, aes(x = .resid)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(100000),
                     labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of residuals",
       x = "Residual", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```
]

- Residuals are centred on zero and roughly symmetric, but **spread out more for expensive houses**
- Typical prediction error (residual standard error): about **`r dollar(round(final_fit$sigma, -1))`**

---

# Conclusions and limitations

.pull-left[
### What we found

- **Quality and size** drive house prices in Ames most strongly
- Together, area, bedrooms, quality and kitchens explain about **`r round(100 * final_fit$r.squared)`%** of price variation
- Newer and remodelled houses sell for more, but less strongly than size
- More bedrooms or kitchens *at the same size* go with lower prices
]

.pull-right[
### Limitations

- **Location** (neighbourhood) was not included and likely explains much of the remaining ~`r round(100 * (1 - final_fit$r.squared))`%
- Wider spread for expensive houses: a log-price model might fit better
- Bedrooms and area are correlated, which makes their separate effects harder to read
- One town, sales from `r min(data$Yr.Sold)` to `r max(data$Yr.Sold)` only: results may not generalise
]

---
